title: Poll suggests slight majority of UCP voters favour separation as party stares down ‘tough days’ ahead
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Poll suggests slight majority of UCP voters favour separation as party stares down ‘tough days’ ahead

A new poll suggests the group with the highest level of support for Alberta separation is supporters of the United Conservative Party, trumping other groups, including those defined by age, religiosity and education.

Actual Article Body:
As part of her latest round of polling, Janet Brown sought to understand the factors driving support for separatism in advance of Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum.

She found most support wasn’t found amongst people who live outside the major cities.

It wasn’t the majority opinion of people with a certain level of education.

Nor was it of those who work a certain type of job or make a certain amount of money.

The group where the highest levels of support for Option 2 was found? Supporters of the United Conservative Party.

“It is a hot potato for the UCP and Danielle Smith. It is that part of the voting public that is split on this issue,” she said.

On Oct. 19, voters will be asked whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada, or whether the Government of Alberta should hold a second, binding referendum to separate from Canada.

Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

Everything you need to know about the 10 questions in Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum

Among those polled who said they would vote for the United Conservative Party, 53 per cent said they’d vote for the separation option. Forty per cent said they’d vote to stay in Canada.

That trumped all demographic groups studied by Brown and her team.

Compared to the 53 per cent of UCP supporters in favour of the separation option, 25 per cent of respondents in small centres said they’d vote for Option 2 on Oct. 19.

Twenty-eight per cent of those with a high school education or less supported the separation option, while 30 per cent of those with college or some university said the same.

At 98 per cent, nearly all respondents who said they would vote for the Alberta NDP if an election were held today said they wanted to stay in Canada.

“I’m a little bit surprised to see them that high in the UCP, very admittedly,” Travis Toews told CBC News of the numbers.

Toews was Alberta's minister of finance from 2019 to 2023. He’s one of the signatories to the federalist initiative known as Lead Not Leave.

He sees “lingering scar tissue” in the party tied to former federal policy.

“I think many of us were disillusioned during those years,” Toews said.

But he argued conditions have improved under Prime Minister Mark Carney.

“It’s a different day. We now have … the majority of Canadians supporting energy development and pipelines,” he said.

“Over time, we can agree with a majority of Canadians on key economic issues that not only will affect Alberta's prosperity down the road, but quite frankly, the whole nation's.”

Still, Toews sees the political clouds swirling. The divide between the two camps in the party poses challenges in advance of the next election, in his view.

“I think if we continue to have a preoccupation — if right of centre provincial political parties continue to have a fixation with separation and independence — I believe it will make it very difficult for those parties to form government provincially,” he said.

“These are tough days for Premier Smith politically, for sure.”

On Tuesday, Red Deer-South UCP MLA Jason Stephan confirmed to CBC News he has voted in favour of proceeding with a legally binding referendum on whether the province should leave Canada.

“I've always supported having a referendum on independence because I want Ottawa to be compelled to fix the things that are broken," he said.

He added, “I've never said that I want Alberta to separate."

Last month, the Alberta NDP flipped a conservative stronghold with a win in Calgary-Shaw.

Later that week, a UCP riding association in southern Alberta formally urged a party vote to review the premier’s leadership.

“Here’s the reality: this kind of an issue is very divisive. And it’s divisive within communities, within businesses, within families and certainly within constituency associations,” Toews said.

“We need to get through this, past this referendum. I believe that we as Albertans need to rally around the principle of leading, not leaving.”
